title: The Famous Lucena
summary: Prepare a fourth-rank rook bridge, drive the king away and shelter your king from checks.

nodes.question: How can the king make room for c7 to promote?
nodes.explanation: The white king blocks its own pawn, and the defending rook can check from behind. A fourth-rank rook will later interpose and end those checks.

nodes.question: What was the purpose of the rook on e4?
nodes.explanation: White has drawn the checking rook to c1 and reached c5. The prepared rook can now block the file on c4 while protected by the king.

nodes.question: Can exchanging the rooks save Black?
nodes.explanation: The c4 bridge is protected by Kc5. If Black exchanges rooks, the white king recaptures and the c-pawn promotes beyond the black king’s reach.

branches.title: Prepare the bridge before walking the king
commentary: Begin from the source’s five-piece Lucena diagram after ...Rc1. The earlier two-pawn game sequence remains context.
Rd4 puts the rook on the fourth rank in advance, preparing a later shelter from file checks.
Ke7 is the source’s selected waiting king move.
Re4+ checks along the e-file, pushing the defending king farther from c7.
Kf7 moves away. The king is now far enough that a later rook trade cannot stop the pawn.
Kd7 clears c8 so the pawn can promote, but remains ready to answer checks.
Rd1+ starts checking from behind along the d-file.
Kc6 stays near the pawn and heads toward the bridge square.
Rc1+ switches files to follow the king.
Kd6 zigzags away from the check rather than abandoning the prepared fourth rank.
Rd1+ follows onto the d-file again.
Kc5 reaches a square where the king will protect a rook interposition on c4.
Rc1+ is the last illustrated check before White builds the bridge.
Rc4 blocks the check and is protected by Kc5. The selected exact position is winning; the source reports resignation here rather than showing a forced mate.

commentary: This independently completed representative line tests the source’s claim that a rook trade does not save Black.
Rxc4+ removes the bridge rook and checks the white king.
Kxc4 recaptures, reaching a king-and-pawn ending with Black too far from c8.
Ke6 is an independent representative king approach, still outside the pawn’s promotion square.
c8=Q+ promotes with check. The exact queen ending is winning for White; further mating technique is not encoded.

exercises.prompt: Why did the rook go to the fourth rank so early?
exercises.answer: The king needs a protected interposition once it reaches c5. Rc4 ends the checking sequence without giving up the pawn.

exercises.prompt: Why does trading rooks lose for Black?
exercises.answer: Kxc4 leaves the c7 pawn ready to promote, while the black king on f7 cannot reach c8 in time.
